stories.headline: Tarik Skubal's free agency contract, predicted by MLB insiders
stories.summary: How big a deal could the Dodgers ace get and who could sign him? We asked around the sport.
stories.body:
There has been a steady flow of elite free agents -- complete with discussion about where they might land and how big their contracts might be -- during the past few offseasons: Aaron Judge after the 2022 season, Shohei Ohtani after the 2023 season, Juan Soto after the 2024 season (and a postseason update) and then Kyle Schwarber and Kyle Tucker after the 2025 season.

This year's free agent class isn't as good top to bottom as they often are, but there is a clear prize: Los Angeles Dodgers lefty Tarik Skubal, the back-to-back AL Cy Young winner.

There are a lot of intriguing questions around Skubal's potential free agency: Will he deliver in the playoffs for the back-to-back champion Dodgers? How will teams perceive the history of procedures on his arm? Will Skubal's agent Scott Boras pull a rabbit out of his hat? Will Skubal sign before or after the expected lockout coming Dec. 1?

Given all that, it wasn't hard to get industry insiders to discuss his potential contract and the unique conditions he faces.

How much will Skubal get?

Here are the 27 contract projections from the folks I spoke with, broken into tiers of guaranteed money:

Up to $300 million (7)

4 years, $176 million

6 years, $210 million

6 years, $264 million

7 years, $280 million

7 years, $300 million

5 years, $300 million

6 years, $300 million

$300 to 350 million (7)

10 years, $325 million

8 years, $325 million

7 years, $325.5 million

7 years, $330 million

8 years, $340 million

7 years, $350 million

10 years, $350 million

$351 to 400 million (9)

8 years, $352 million

10 years, $360 million

9 years, $387 million

8 years, $400 million

8 years, $400 million

8 years, $400 million

8 years, $400 million

10 years, $400 million

10 years, $400 million

Over $400 million (4)

9 years, $450 million

10 years, $460 million

9 years, $500 million

10 years, $500 million

The average projected contract was eight years and $355 million, which is a $44.6 million average annual value (AAV). Sixteen of 27 projections (59%) were for $325 to 400 million guaranteed over seven to 10 years -- a clear sweet spot, and you'll see below why that is.

I also asked panelists whether the deal would be done before the Dec. 1 expiration of the CBA, when the expected lockout would start: 21 of 27 (78%) predicted the deal will be done before Dec. 1, similar timing to the nine-figure deals of Corey Seager, Marcus Semien, Max Scherzer, Robbie Ray, Kevin Gausman and Javier Baez that came before the 2021-2022 lockout began. Boras negotiated the first three of those contracts.

The key factors

Panelists often mentioned three standards projecting what the Skubal camp will be shooting for: Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 million contract (highest pitcher guarantee), Scherzer's three-year, $130 million deal (highest pitcher AAV at $43.3 million) and Gerrit Cole's nine-year, $324 million deal (the guarantee mark Yamamoto barely beat; many think Skubal will get an inflation-adjusted version of this). Boras was the agent for the Scherzer and Cole deals.

There are two reasons panelists believe there will be a small group of teams bidding near the eventual contract: the history of how nine-figure pitcher deals have worked out and Skubal's injury history. The poor track record of pitcher megadeals is self-explanatory. A vintage one is Corbin Burnes landing $210 million guaranteed and making 14 starts over the first two years of the deal due to various arm issues. In Skubal's case, he had Tommy John surgery in 2016 while in college, a 2022 surgery on the flexor tendon in his throwing elbow and a 2026 procedure to remove a loose elbow particle.

The average age of the 32 prior pitchers to land nine-figure free agent deals was 30, which Skubal will be in a few months. His three-year platform performance entering free agency is among the best of that cohort. His ERA+ trails only Jacob deGrom (who threw less than half as many innings as Skubal in his three-year window) and narrowly falls behind Kevin Brown in 1999, the first to land such a deal.

The contenders

I didn't ask panelists who they believed would sign Skubal, but some volunteered guesses or readings of the market.

Sleepers: The Los Angeles Angels, Chicago White Sox and San Diego Padres were mentioned in this category; the Angels and Padres have new ownership, and the White Sox have a new owner in waiting.

In most high-end free agent bidding processes, there's at least one surprising or mystery team. After circling back with some sources after the projections were in, the Padres seemed to be the consensus pick for the most serious bidder in this group.

True contenders: The Dodgers, Detroit Tigers and New York Mets came up most often for this category, though the Tigers were mentioned as more likely to be on the periphery than a true contender. Most insiders project the Dodgers and Mets to be serious bidders, but there is some hesitation surrounding the Dodgers given the controversy around the team's ownership. Some thought the Mets might be looking to do a shorter-term deal such as they did with Bo Bichette, which might not work if Skubal is looking to set a record for guaranteed money.

The New York Yankees were just behind that lead group in total mentions. For those who thought the Dodgers wouldn't break the bank, and the Mets would only offer AAV-record deals, the Yankees were a common fallback. Brian Cashman has landed Cole, Max Fried and Carlos Rodon in free agency in the last half dozen years and adding Skubal to a group that also includes Cam Schlittler, Ryan Weathers, Will Warren and Clarke Schmidt would give the Yankees the best starting pitching in the sport. That much depth likely would necessitate a trade.

Skubal's strategy

There were some projections of opt-outs, with four panelists laying out a contract with multiple opt-outs. Deferrals also came up from four panelists. Although there is some suspicion they might be outlawed in the new CBA, there also was general agreement that Boras and Skubal will be going for the biggest total guarantee, which can be juiced on paper with deferrals.

Opt-outs and deferrals are two common levers for agents to pull in free agent contract negotiations, but Skubal's specific situation might include another notable lever: a big signing bonus. One panelist thought Skubal would get almost 20% of the guarantee from his projected contract in the form of a signing bonus, half of that payable before the Dec. 1 expiration of the current CBA.

The thinking behind that would be to 1) be sure to be paid this year, even if a season doesn't happen and 2) if a season is shortened and salaries are paid pro rata, the bonus wouldn't be reduced the way a salary would be. There are also possible personal tax advantages to Skubal if he's paid before playing for a new team, which could have higher state income taxes than where he lives in the offseason. An agent summed up the strategy: "As much up front as possible ... not sure if owners will allow it."

Skubal's injury history also was a point of discussion, with the belief he could go for a shorter-term deal and shoot for the AAV record. If his long-term options aren't to his liking, could a team come in with four years, $200 million with opt-outs and injury language (a year added to the deal at a lower salary if he has an elbow surgery, for example)?

Panelists largely thought Skubal would go for the biggest total guarantee, but when I floated the AAV-buster scenario, a strategy that the Mets employed to land Bichette last winter, many reconsidered. Maybe a few teams take that approach, and Skubal's process plays out like Tucker's free agency last offseason, when he signed a four-year, $240 million deal with the Dodgers.

The final thing to consider is simply how many teams will be bidders above the $325 million mark, which is widely believed to be the first standard Skubal wants to clear. It's always hard to predict these things as it's an ownership-level call, but the list of clubs that would pay the expected market price for a long-term deal on a 30-year-old pitcher with three procedures on an elbow can't be long. Some teams will be philosophically out due to years, position and age, but Skubal and Boras need only two teams to make a bidding war possible. Based on the previous free agent contract polls I've done, clearly the best player on the market tends to overperform the projections.

stories.headline: Where NBA expansion stands ahead of the 2026-27 season
stories.summary: As NBA training camps begin for 30 teams, here's the latest intel on the potential for the 31st and 32nd teams.
stories.body:
NBA commissioner Adam Silver's news conference in December 2020 was remarkable for several reasons. Similar to many large gatherings during the depth of the COVID-19 pandemic, it was conducted entirely on Zoom. But it was also when he was first asked whether the NBA would consider expansion again for the first time in two decades.

The question, from then-ESPN reporter Tim Bontemps, was framed as a discussion of how the league might recover some of the revenue lost during the pandemic. Silver responded that expansion wasn't on "the front burner," but added that it was "sort of the manifest destiny of the league."

In other words, expansion was inevitable. The only question was when.

First, the NBA focused on securing its new 11-year, $76 billion broadcast deal. Then, it turned its attention to expansion. That process is now nearing its conclusion, with ESPN's Shams Charania reporting this week that the league is expected to select the winning bid for ownership of the Las Vegas team in the very near future, from among three finalist groups.

Here's our latest intel from sources around the NBA on how the final stages of this six-year process could play out.

Where does expansion stand heading into the 2026-27 NBA season?
Silver said he wants a vote on expansion before the end of this calendar year.

That's a broad enough statement to leave a lot of room for negotiations. As it stands, the NBA and strategic adviser PJT Partners, which is handling the process, are more focused on getting a team in Las Vegas, where the interest and bidding have been far more robust than in Seattle.

The expectation is the Las Vegas franchise will go for around $10 billion, with the winning group also expected to spend an additional $2-3 billion to construct a new arena.

As Silver mentioned, there is still discussion among current owners and the bid groups about the best place for a new arena.

A vote on the three groups bidding on Las Vegas -- Nancy Walton Laurie and Bill Laurie; Steve Apostolopoulos and Marc Lasry; and Bill Foley and Jerry Colangelo -- could come soon, sources told Charania.

The runner-up groups could then pivot to Seattle, where Kraken owner Samantha Holloway's group appears to be in pole position, with a valuation sources with knowledge of the process currently estimate to be around $6 billion.

Holloway has tremendous leverage because her company, One Roof Sports & Entertainment, has a majority share of Climate Pledge Arena, which already hosts the WNBA's Seattle Storm and the Kraken and could easily convert to host NBA games as well.

Any other bidder would either have to build their own arena or negotiate with Holloway to use Climate Pledge Arena, a state-of-the-art arena built in 2021, which has also hosted NCAA tournament games. It should be pointed out, though, that the city of Seattle included a provision in its initial 2018 deal with the Oak View Group that if Seattle is awarded an NBA franchise in the future, the new owner had an option to buy into the arena management entity of the arena at fair market value.

There's also a possibility that the runner-ups in Vegas will pivot -- as Josh Kushner and Bob Iger did in buying the Los Angeles Lakers from Mark Walter in August -- and try to buy an existing team.

Several ownership-level sources say the most interesting fallout from the decision on Las Vegas is how it could impact the situation with the Portland Trail Blazers and new owner Tom Dundon.

The Seattle market is closest to Portland, meaning a new team there could diminish the Blazers' overall market.

But it also serves as a relocation threat for Dundon, giving him leverage in his negotiations with local authorities on renovations to the Moda Center or a new arena.

So ... what's the latest on the Portland situation?
Now, this is where it gets interesting. Dundon is in a standoff with the city of Portland regarding a renovation of the Moda Center and has used the expansion process and the threat of relocation for leverage in recent discussions with other owners and city officials, according to multiple ownership and industry sources.

Though Silver has publicly stated that he'd consider relocating the Blazers as "a failure," Dundon's threat is real as long as Seattle and Vegas are being considered as NBA markets and Dundon has issues with his current arena.

Still, expansion is far more likely than relocation.

Recent NFL relocation fees for the Los Angeles Rams and Los Angeles Chargers were $645 million, while the Raiders paid $378 million to move to Vegas.

Even adjusted for the exponential growth in valuation since those moves, one industry source estimated a relocation fee in the NBA would be $1.5 billion-2 billion, if the other owners were even willing to consider it.

Divided by 30, that's a fraction of what the owners stand to make in expansion fees.

Also, why would the other owners vote for relocation for an owner who has been in the league for only a year?

What does the formal approval process look like?

Twenty-three of the 30 owners (two-thirds) must vote to approve the concept of expansion and whichever bid groups are chosen for expansion.

Though there is a lot of momentum for expansion, support for it is not universal, multiple ownership and industry sources say.

Some owners have expressed concerns about the dilution of talent and revenue across the league if two franchises are added.

Others have more personal concerns about how these two franchises could affect their current regional markets.

For example, the Utah Jazz, Denver Nuggets, Phoenix Suns and both Los Angeles teams have fans in Las Vegas, and a new team in Seattle could theoretically draw fans away from Portland, Minnesota or Denver.

Though there remains a group of owners who aren't fully convinced the league should expand at this time, sources indicate there's still confidence that expansion will pass -- with either Silver or other owners whipping the votes.

If the franchises combine to generate $15 billion-18 billion in expansion fees, each of the 30 owners stands to make approximately $500-600 million before the new teams begin play in 2028-29. One owner told ESPN his franchise was already monitoring how expansion fees could impact them.

These expansion fees are not considered basketball-related income and thus are not shared with the players. This was a major point of contention in recent WNBA collective bargaining negotiations.

Expansion fees are considered compensation for diluting future revenues from 30 owners to 32 owners. Dropping from 1/30th to 1/32nd of that pool creates a revenue loss of roughly $9 million in national broadcast revenue, per team, per year. Dilution also impacts distributions of league sponsorships, merchandise and local broadcast revenue, which is reported as BRI and international licensing.

Why is the Las Vegas expansion process currently ahead of Seattle's?

Market forces. In Las Vegas, there are three groups aggressively bidding for the franchise.

Competition creates leverage and demand, whereas Seattle's final price largely comes down to whether the NBA can create more competition for Holloway's group, which includes philanthropist Melinda French Gates and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, to increase the price.

There is one other publicly known bidder in Seattle, BlackSun Private Equity group, which announced that it had joined the Tulalip Tribes on a bid featuring a new arena built in a massive entertainment district 35 miles north of the city. However, industry sources have indicated that there's at least one other group that has expressed interest in Seattle that hasn't been publicly identified.

Why is there so much more interest in Vegas? Seattle is a top-15 media market with 4 million residents with massive corporate wealth -- anchored by companies such as Microsoft, Amazon and Costco.

Las Vegas has only 2.3 million residents and is a top-40 media market. But with 38 million annual visitors, it's also a global entertainment capital.

A new NBA franchise would be a boon to tourism, similar to what the Raiders have been since they relocated from Oakland. Las Vegas's support for the Aces and Golden Knights is also notable in the NBA's consideration of it as a market.

Where does the latest expansion news leave Seattle?

Seattle remains in a bit of a holding pattern until Las Vegas is settled.

Holloway's group doesn't want to bid against itself if it doesn't have to. The question is whether a runner-up in Vegas would pivot to the Seattle market and create more robust competition.

Foley is a Vegas resident with strong ties to the city as the owner of the Las Vegas Knights of the NHL. Laurie lives in Henderson, Nev., so neither of them would have an easy time pivoting to a different market after so much focus on Las Vegas.

That leaves the Apostolopolous group, which is based in Toronto, and partnered with former Milwaukee Bucks owner Marc Lasry, who lives in New York. Steve Apostolopolous previously bid on the Charlotte Hornets and the Washington Commanders, showing a willingness to bid on franchises across different sports and markets.

Would the NBA have to add two teams if it is to expand? Could it expand to 31?
The NBA can do whatever it wants, but expanding by one franchise would leave an odd number of teams and unbalance the schedule. But there is precedent.

In fact, from 1980, when the Dallas Mavericks were added to the league, until 2004, when the Charlotte Bobcats were added, the NBA had an odd number of teams.

The WNBA, where the Golden State Valkyries were announced in October 2023, became the league's 13th franchise while debuting in the 2025 season.

Toronto and Portland were awarded in 2024 and made their debuts as the 14th and 15th franchises this season. But the WNBA doesn't use the traditional playoff structure of Eastern Conference versus Western Conference.

The top eight teams make the playoffs, regardless of conference affiliation.

stories.headline: FA: Man City verdict has 'significant implications for integrity of game'
stories.summary: The Football Association have expressed their concern that the guilty charge aimed at Manchester City over the Premier League's financial rules stains the "integrity" of the game.
stories.body:
The Football Association expressed its concern that the guilty charge aimed at Manchester City over the Premier League's financial rules stains the "integrity" of the game.

The FA's full statement read: "The Independent Commission's decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game. We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate.

"As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage. We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely."

Friday is the deadline for City to appeal the guilty verdict into their breaches of Premier League rules. They have stated that they intend to appeal.

The commission concluded more than £830 million ($1.1 bn) of such funding was used to inflate revenues and enable the club to comply with Premier League and UEFA financial rules through a series of "sham" arrangements.

The 40-page core decision published Tuesday shows the independent commission rejected the CPC explanation as "untrue" in its findings, adding: "We concluded that it was an 'explanation' that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the disguised funding scheme."

Sponsor Etihad Airways, which is owned by an Abu Dhabi fund chaired by City owner Sheikh Mansour's brother, is considering legal action against the Premier League.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC earlier this week that he would be concerned if City's owners sold the club due to the guilty verdict because they have been "a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester." But a No. 10 Downing Street spokesman afterwards: "As the Prime Minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules.

"He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

- Manchester City guilty charges explained: Premier League's options, how appeal works, more

- How Man City players, staff are handling Premier League verdict

- Klopp not preparing for more titles after verdict against Man City

But Jamie Carragher wrote for The Telegraph: "The club can only heal and recover from the shame of their guilt once the custodians recognise they have failed in their duty and sell up."

Gary Neville insisted the entire league has suffered due to City's guilty verdict, saying on the Stick To Football podcast on Disney+: "To listen to this, it is chilling.

"We always think that we've got an enormous integrity, the Premier League, that we are the sort of league that sets the standard, and that it's other leagues that have got corruption, fraud, doping scandals, match-fixing, referee scandals.

"This is now coming to our country. This is now coming to our league. This is the greatest export that we have in our country. At the moment we're being dragged through the mud."

Press Association contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Charles Leclerc tops second practice, Mercedes off the pace
stories.summary: Charles Leclerc topped the timesheets in second practice at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with the session staying dry despite the threat of rain.
stories.body:
Charles Leclerc topped the timesheets in second practice at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with the session staying dry despite the threat of rain.

The Ferrari driver set the time halfway through the session on the soft compound tyre and crossed the line 0.099 seconds ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

McLaren's Lando Norris was third-fastest, with Max Verstappen behind. The Dutchamn, who was fastest in first practice, spent the session doing long runs on the medium tyre, while the majority of the grid were on the soft tyres.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton rounded out the top five and was three-tenths off his teammate Leclerc's pace.

McLaren made some adjustments to Norris' rear wing to get the 'Macarena' style rear wing that Oscar Piastri was using in first practice on Friday.

Piastri ended the second session in sixth, while Mercedes duo George Russell and title leader Kimi Antonelli were off the pace and finished down in seventh and eighth respectively. Both drivers were on soft tyres but had to abort their flying laps.

- Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Max Verstappen leads first practice from George Russell

- Why is the Bahrain Grand Prix taking place in Malaysia, 4,000 miles away? F1's unusual race explained

- Lewis Hamilton hits out at Ferrari hierarchy in Fred Vasseur defence: 'Point fingers somewhere else'

Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto complained on the team radio that Hamilton got in his way on track when he was on a quick lap, while the seven-time champion reported that "he can't see through" his right mirror. Hamilton is under investigation by the stewards.

Bortoleto also brought out the Virtual Safety Car in the closing stages of the session.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson was ninth and Alpine's Pierre Gasly rounded out the top 10.

stories.headline: A'ja Wilson stars as Aces oust Fever from WNBA playoffs
stories.summary: A'ja Wilson made sure her basketball spoke for itself Thursday night, as the four-time WNBA MVP scored 36 points to lead the defending champion Las Vegas Aces to a 94-83 victory over the Indiana Fever in the deciding Game 3 of the first round.
stories.body:
LAS VEGAS -- A'ja Wilson could have used Tuesday's confrontation with a fan in Indiana to fire her up for the deciding Game 3 of her Las Vegas Aces' first-round WNBA playoff series with the Indiana Fever.

But she said she really didn't do that. Instead, she focused on taking care of business. Wilson had 36 points and 10 rebounds in the No. 3 seed Aces' 94-83 victory over the No. 6 seed Fever on Thursday at Michelob Ultra Arena.

"I have my days. I have my moments because I'm human," Wilson said about the incident in the Ace's Game 2 loss in Indianapolis, where she earned a technical foul but no subsequent discipline from the league.

"But after a while, I understood I didn't want to be a distraction to myself and my team. And I knew what we had to do coming into tonight. So I put it behind me."

The Aces put the Fever behind them and moved on to the WNBA semifinals for the eighth season in a row. They await Friday's winner of Game 3 of the Dallas-Golden State series.

The Aces will start that best-of-five series in San Francisco if the No. 2 seed Valkyries win or Las Vegas will host Games 1 and 2 if the No. 7 Wings prevail. Either way, the Aces are in familiar territory, having won three of the past four WNBA championships.

They advanced Thursday in the same way they've claimed those titles: Wilson led the way, with guards Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young alongside her contributing. This is the sixth season the trio has played together for the Aces.

Before Game 3, Las Vegas starting forward Stephanie Talbot was ruled out because of a leg injury. Guard Jewell Loyd moved into the starting lineup, and Aces coach Becky Hammon let Gray and Young know to prepare for a long work shift.

"I just told them to be ready to run 40," Hammon said. "You're not coming out until you tell me you need [to]."

Young and Gray indeed played 40 minutes, combining for 41 points, 12 assists and 12 rebounds. Wilson played 37 minutes, and Loyd -- who had 11 points -- played 35.

The Aces know their way around the game this time of year, showing a little gamesmanship. About three minutes after the tip, Aces forward Brianna Turner appeared to deliberately walk into the Fever's on-court huddle and got a reaction out of Clark, who pushed her out of it. Both were given technical fouls.

It didn't rattle Clark, who was playing in just her fifth playoff game. She had 11 points in the first quarter as both teams were on fire offensively and ended the period tied at 31. But the Aces outscored the Fever 23-17 in the second quarter.

Indiana closed to within 82-80 with three minutes left on Kelsey Mitchell's 3-pointer. But after the Fever got the ball back, Mitchell missed a shot and then was called for a loose ball foul that the Fever challenged. The challenge was unsuccessful, and all the momentum went back to the Aces.

Mitchell finished with 23 points, Aliyah Boston had 19 and Clark had 18 for Indiana.

"You've got to give credit to the Aces," Clark said. "I thought they played well. I thought they were ready to go, and that's what championship teams do."

Wilson and the Aces are seeking their fourth WNBA title, which would tie them for most with the Minnesota Lynx, Seattle Storm and Houston Comets. Wilson, who is expected to be named the WNBA's MVP for the fifth time, said Tuesday's confrontation is not something she will dwell upon.

"I prayed a lot. I cried a lot," Wilson said of the time between the high emotions of Game 2 and her laser focus to start Game 3. "I talked to a lot of different people, and the amount of love that I received today, the amount of Bible verses that I received, it reminded me I'm covered.

"So I can't really worry about anything else. I'm grateful to be surrounded by people that could constantly lift me up. Once I put that on the back burner, I had to come up. I had to show up for my team today, and I'm glad we got the win."

stories.headline: AFL player movement tracker: trade requests, free agency latest, who's on the move?
stories.summary: The offseason is upon us which means AFL trades, free agency, and player movement is about to take off. Here's the latest news, whispers, and confirmed deals.
stories.body:
It's AFL player movement season, with trades and free agency set to dominate the month of October. So who is going where? Keep track with our player movement guide here.

When is the AFL trade and free agency window?
The 2026 AFL trade period commences on Monday, October 5 and closes in the evening of Wednesday, October 14.

The free agency window opens and closes a little earlier; it runs from Friday, October 2 until Friday, October 9.

Friday, Oct. 2
FREE AGENCY OPEN
Greene on his way to the Cats

Toby Greene will join Geelong as an unrestricted free agent on a three-year deal, re-partnering with former Giants teammate Jeremey Cameron.

The paperwork was lodged to the AFL on Friday morning.

The Giants receive band three compensation for Greene, which is currently pick No. 26 in the upcoming draft.

Greene departs the Giants with his name etched in the club's record books, sitting first in games played for the club with a tally of 282 games, as well as leading the club's all-time goalkicking tally with 450 majors.

Briggs now a Tiger

Richmond has landed GWS ruck Kieren Briggs as an unrestricted free agent.

Briggs' move to the Tigers was confirmed just hours after the free agency window opened on Friday.

Briggs played 88 games for GWS after joining the club as the No.34 pick in the 2018 draft.

Amartey officially joins the Blues

Free agency has opened with a bang, with out-of-favour key forward Joel Amartey committing to Carlton.

Details are still to come on the length of contract, and Sydney's compensation.

Hawthorn father-son recommits despite interest

Calsher Dear has made a shock decision to re-sign with the Hawks for two years, despite being out of favour thorughout 2026.

The 20-year-old has kicked 39 goals from 31 games, but found himself behind Jack Gunston, Mitch Lewis and Mabior Chol. With Gunston signed on and Suns forward Ben King expected to sign with the Hawks as well, there were questions about whether Dear would get enough opportunity at his childhood club.

Hawks list boss Mark McKenzie said the club was "really pleased" that Dear had recommitted.

"He remains an important part of what we are trying to achieve as a club," he said.

"Following his debut season, Calsher showed us all the special talent that he is, but as a key tall at 21 years of age, we've needed to be patient with his progression.

"Having battled several injuries over his first three seasons in the system, we are very excited about what the future holds for Calsher with a strong pre-season under his belt and greater continuity into 2027 and beyond."

Thursday, Oct. 1
Goater set to make cross-city switch

North Melbourne defender Josh Goater is set to join the Hawks after requesting a trade on Thursday.

Having played just 18 games, the 23-year-old had fallen out of favour after an injury-hit run in his time at North.

Premiership Lion requests trade

The Brisbane Lions have confirmed Sam Marshall has requested a trade to St Kilda.

"The Brisbane Lions confirm premiership midfielder Sam Marshall has requested to be traded to St Kilda," the Lions said in a statement.

"Marshall has played 13 games, including the 2025 Premiership, across two seasons since being selected in the first round of the 2024 draft as a graduate of the Youi Brisbane Lions Academy.

"The club respects Marshall's request to be traded, and will work towards facilitating an outcome that best reflects true value to the Brisbane Lions for the 20-year-old."

Tuesday, Sept. 29

Two-time Brownlow Medal winner Lachie Neale has told Brisbane he will depart the club as an unrestricted free agent and sign a three-year deal with Collingwood.

Aware that Neale intended to leave at the end of the year, the Lions never offered him a new contract.

The paperwork for the deal is expected to be formalised as early as Friday when the free agency period opens.

Friday, Sept. 25

Zak Butters isn't the only South Australian-based player keen to join the Western Bulldogs, with Crows' key defender Jordon Butts officially naming the Dogs as his preferred offseason destination.

Wantaway Sydney forward Joel Amartey has confirmed his desire to join Carlton as an unrestricted free agent.

With Charlie Curnow (75 goals in 2026) and Logan McDonald (51) cementing their spots in the Sydney forward line as the prime targets, Amartey is hoping for more opportunity at the Blues.

Thursday, Sept. 17
GWS captain finally makes big call on his future

Toby Greene has opted to leave GWS, telling the AFL club he wishes to play with Geelong next season. Greene, who has been at the Giants since their foundation season in 2012, wants to go back to Victoria for family reasons.

In an extraordinary way to announce the decision, outgoing GWS boss Dave Matthews confirmed Greene's intentions on radio, before the club released a statement.

The 32-year-old has been offered a lucrative three-year deal to join the Cats.

Saturday, Sept. 12
Zak Butters makes huge free agency call
The year's hottest restricted free agent Zak Butters has made a huge call on his future, nominating the Western Bulldogs as his preferred destination.

After a year of speculation, with Geelong thought to be the front-runner for the Power star's signature, Butters made the call on Saturday, first reported by AFL.com.au's Callum Twomey.

The deal is reportedly for nine years.

Thursday, Sept. 10
Hogan set to join Pies
GWS and Collingwood have both confirmed that 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan has chosen the Magpies at his next home.

Set to be a four-club player, Hogan is 31 and coming off a 12-goal season from just nine appearances.

Brisbane's Zac Bailey has ended months of 'will he, won't he' speculation to sign with the Lions for eight years, taking him through the 2034 season, the the club confirmed on Tuesday.

"I'm absolutely rapt to be staying at the Brisbane Lions," Bailey said in a statement.

"I love the environment here, the players, coaches and staff who all make it a great place to be and I feel like this Club continues to bring the best out of me.

"This Club means so much to me - I came here as a young player and have grown up here and to know I will be here long-term is something I'm really proud of.

"I love what we as a club have achieved during my time here and I am super excited about what we can continue to achieve together."

Rowan Marshall requests trade
St Kilda ruck Rowan Marshall looks set to be on the move, with the Saints confirming the big man had requested a trade for the second straight season.

While Marshall hasn't requested a specific club, it's likely to be Geelong after he failed to secure a trade to the Cats last year. He played 21 games for the Saints this seaosn, juggling ruck duties with Tom De Koning, who came in from Carlton last offseason.

"Rowan is a highly valued member of the St Kilda Football Club and remains contracted until the end of 2027," the Saints said in a statement.

The No. 4 pick in the 2023 AFL draft Zane Duursma has requested a trade out of North Melbourne, with Melbourne in his sights.

The news comes a week after coach Alastair Clarkson was sacked by the club. North won nine games in 2026, their best return since 2019.

After speculation about his future at the Magpies, mdifielder Ed Allan has put pen to paper, signing a four year extension to remain at Collingwood.

According to afl.com.au, both Arty Jones and Buku Khamis will remain at the Kennel this offseason.

Jones will sign a three-year deal, while Khamis has a five-year contract in front of him.

Essendon and Brisbane had interest in livewire forward Jones, who had a standout performance against Collingwood in the wildcard final win, while the Blues were heavily linked to Khamis for a second straight offseason.

A big boost for the Hawks, with club champion Luke Hodge's son Cooper choosing to join the Melbourne-based team as a father-son at this year's draft.

He had the option of going to Brisbane as a Lions academy member.

stories.headline: UFC 332 preview and picks: Why haven't there been more women's fights?
stories.summary: Top storylines and coaches' analysis for UFC 332 in Salt Lake City.
stories.body:
For all of the growth and progress of women's MMA over the past 15 years, the 2026 schedule has raised an uncomfortable -- but glaring -- question: What is happening to women's fights? Saturday's UFC 332 event in Salt Lake City will mark the first UFC event this year headlined by women, when Natalia Silva (20-5-1) and Wang Cong (10-1) meet for the vacant flyweight title. This year's lack of high-profile women's fights (and the excitement that should accompany them) has been impossible to miss. Wang, the 34-year-old Chinese challenger, has certainly felt it in the buildup to Saturday.

"Everyone was talking about how bad this main event is," Wang told ESPN, through an interpreter. "Of course I know about it. I think me and my opponent will prove them wrong, and show this is a fight they need to watch."

The sport could definitely use a boost. According to ESPN Research, the UFC has promoted 415 total bouts this year; 56 have featured women. That 13% split is the lowest mark in a decade.

The last women's fight to headline any UFC event was a non-title bout between Mackenzie Dern and Amanda Ribas in January 2025. For the last women's fight to headline a numbered event, one has to go all the way back to a bantamweight title fight between Amanda Nunes and Irene Aldana in June 2023.

Those trends are unlikely to change if some of the more underlying metrics continue to hold. Women's fights are increasingly being pushed to the prelims portion of events. In 2026, 83% of women's fights have appeared on prelims, compared with 72% in 2024, 61% in 2021 and 54% in 2017.

For their part, both Wang and Silva, a 29-year-old challenger out of Brazil, are predicting a memorable matchup Saturday. Wang is a former professional kickboxer with an aggressive style. Silva is known as more of a matador, but in 2024 when she went against Jessica Andrade, the most aggressive opponent of her UFC career, they won fight of the night.

"For sure, it's going to be a well-fought battle," Silva told ESPN through an interpreter. "She comes in aggressive, which gives me the opportunity to be aggressive as well. What I can tell people is that's going to be an incredible fight."

One thing is undeniable, Wang and Silva have a rare opportunity on Saturday to headline a numbered event with a women's title fight.

More storylines to watch
Gautier is getting the step up in competition he asked for
Ateba Gautier is an athletic, 24-year-old wrecking ball from Cameroon with a 5-0 record in the UFC that includes four knockouts. The combined record of his opponents, however, has been 4-14. That doesn't diminish what Gautier has done, but it's still unknown how he will fare against tougher competition.

For his part, Gautier isn't shying away from challenging himself. Immediately following his last win in May, Gautier called for a fight with former middleweight champion Israel Adesanya -- arguably the greatest 185-pound fighter of all time. The UFC didn't give him Adesanya, but he did get Roman Kopylov, a 35-year-old Russian with 12 UFC bouts. A win wouldn't validate Gautier as a title contender, but it would prove he's ready for greater tests.

Wint could be the sleeper breakout candidate of the card
In terms of fighters who can make an individual splash at UFC 332, Wang and Silva in the main event stand out. Payton Talbott taking on a former champion in Deiveson Figueiredo is an obvious one. Undefeated Jacobe Smith is a finishing machine, and the aforementioned Gautier is in the biggest fight of his career.

Quietly, Anthony Wint could steal the show. Wint's prelim fight against Lucas Armand will be his third in less than two months. He's a former collegiate and NFL linebacker, fighting out of a notoriously talented and striking-oriented gym in Kill Cliff FC. He already is very much on UFC CEO Dana White's radar, having earned his contract on "Contender Series" on Aug. 11. If he does something spectacular, expect White to give it attention in his postfight comments (which in turn, draws everyone's attention).

Coaches' questions for women's flyweight championship
'What is Natalia Silva's game plan under pressure?'

Cong's striking is on point. She is aggressive with it, but she makes mistakes with it as well. I feel like Silva is the more well-rounded fighter, and it's up to her to take advantage of that. If this fight does go to the ground, I think Silva will present bigger problems -- and I see that as a path to victory for her. Wang is going to look for the knockout, and because of that, she will overextend in certain positions. I have a gut feeling Silva is going to work some ground work into this one. Silva is so good at controlling the pace of a fight, but with Cong coming at her so aggressively, I think she'll be forced to try different stuff. It's a pick 'em fight. -- John Wood, Syndicate MMA

Who will own the 'second exchange'?
Silva's path to victory is about space, timing and making Wang reset. Silva needs to use her movement and feints to keep Wang from getting comfortable and building combinations. Silva is best at range, not standing in the pocket. Her counters matter in this matchup. She doesn't just survive Wang's pressure, she scores with midrange kicks and southpaw counters after Wang overcommits. For Wang, it's about pressure without chasing. She needs to cut the cage. Containing Silva becomes the real job. This is where her low kick and body work become weapons. Silva's movement is a huge part of her defense. If Wang can consistently attack the legs and body, she can start shrinking the cage without simply chasing. Who controls what happens after the initial exchange? If Wang attacks, Silva counters and exits, that's Silva's fight. If Wang attacks, Silva tries to exit and Wang cuts her off, those are the moments Wang wants. Whoever imposes their will on that second exchange wins. -- Eric Nicksick, Xtreme Couture

stories.headline: UEFA receives Real Madrid dossier on Barcelona-Negreira case
stories.summary: UEFA has received "a substantial amount of documents" from Real Madrid related to its ongoing inquiry into the Negreira case, European football's governing body said on Thursday.
stories.body:
MADRID -- UEFA has received "a substantial amount of documents" from Real Madrid related to its ongoing inquiry into the Negreira case, European football's governing body said on Thursday.

Payments made by Barcelona to companies linked to José María Enriquez Negreira -- the former vice-president of Spain's Technical Committee of Referees -- over two decades have been subject to a UEFA investigation since 2023, while there is also an ongoing Spanish criminal case.

Barcelona have said the payments, which totaled over €7 million ($7.9m), were made for technical refereeing reports.

- Ronaldo's Portugal walkout is nothing new; he has a long history of rows with coaches

- Source: Mbappé to be available for Clásico

- Raphinha back at Barça, injured in Brazil game

"UEFA can confirm that it has received from Real Madrid CF a substantial amount of documents related to the ongoing investigation into FC Barcelona in the matter involving José María Enríquez Negreira," UEFA confirmed in a statement on Thursday.

"The UEFA Ethics and Disciplinary Inspectors have also received these latest documents which they will assess as part of their ongoing review."

Real Madrid said the dossier included "extensive documentation and evidence regarding events of extraordinary seriousness, which directly affect the integrity of the competition and confidence in the refereeing system."

"Real Madrid C.F. considers it essential that, now that UEFA has this documentation, the investigation proceeds with the utmost urgency until its full conclusion, and that the competent bodies take the appropriate decisions in accordance with the severity of the verified facts," the club said.

"Our club will continue to actively collaborate with UEFA and take all actions within its power to clarify events that it deems incompatible with the principles of integrity, transparency, and fair play that should govern European football."

In May, Madrid president Florentino Pérez said that the club was gathering evidence to submit a dossier to UEFA.

Having previously adopted a conciliatory tone with Barcelona -- saying in 2024 that the two clubs "have to help each other" as they worked together on the proposed European Super League -- Pérez has since been extremely critical of his LaLiga rivals.

"They've stolen seven league [titles] from me," Pérez said in May.

In a statement, Barcelona emphasized that Thursday's development did not equate to "any new proceedings."

"The proceedings were initiated in 2023, with the appointment of two investigators who have since carried out the action they deemed appropriate," Barcelona said. "The Club has always complied with all their requests. These proceedings have not been reopened because they have never been closed.

"The UEFA statement confirms receipt of documentation submitted by Real Madrid and indicates that the investigators will assess it within the framework of the existing investigation. The same text expressly refers, on two occasions, to an investigation and a review that are 'ongoing.' It therefore does not announce the opening, reopening, or reactivation of any proceedings, nor does it contain any assessment of the substance or value of the documentation provided.

"It is up to the investigators to determine what action, if any, they consider appropriate regarding this documentation. As of today, they have not made any new requests to FC Barcelona nor have they forwarded Real Madrid's complaint to the Club. Should they do so, the Club will respond accordingly, as it has done up to now.

"In accordance with the applicable legislation governing this matter, these proceedings are subject to the outcome of the criminal case currently being heard in Spain and will continue to be so."

stories.headline: Concussed Roosters star learns Grand Final fate
stories.summary: Sydney Roosters utility Connor Watson will miss the NRL grand final after failing to receive the green light to return to play inside the code's 11-day concussion stand-down period.
stories.body:
Sydney Roosters utility Connor Watson will miss the NRL Grand Final after failing to receive the green light to return to play inside the code's 11-day concussion stand-down period.

In a cruel blow, Watson will miss Sunday's decider against his former club Newcastle and become the first player to sit out a grand final as a result of a concussion.

Watson was dazed and was taken from the field moments after coming on in the Roosters' preliminary final win over the Dolphins.

Under the NRL's protocol, players diagnosed with a category-one concussion, as Watson was, face a mandatory stand-down period of 11 days.

The Roosters had indicated that Watson was testing well leading into Thursday when the 30-year-old met with an independent specialist.

But on Friday the club confirmed the utility had failed to receive clearance to line up in the grand final.

The outcome means Watson has played his last game for the Roosters with the popular utility heading to St George Illawarra next season before linking up with the PNG Chiefs in 2028.

Watson's absence likely forces Roosters coach Trent Robinson's hand when it comes to his bench, with hooker Benaiah Ioelu the most obvious man to come into Easts' 19-man squad.

Ioelu has played mostly off the bench through his 17-game NRL career and would act as cover for Reece Robson.

"I don't think it takes too much to work out what plan B is, but we have got some really good hookers," Robinson said on Thursday.

"Benaiah Ioelu played some great footy for us this year. He brings a lot of energy to us as well so he will come into consideration then."

Newcastle, meanwhile, are also expected to face a tough decision leading into Sunday's decider as they weigh up a replacement for suspended No. 9 Phoenix Crossland.

Harrison Graham has excelled as a bench option at hooker for the Knights, but coach Justin Holbrook, who doesn't have to name his final team until 90 minutes before kick-off on Sunday, has the option of also starting Thomas Cant or Diesel Hagan.

stories.headline: What to know before setting your lineup for Week 4: Mariota, Tuten in store for breakout week
stories.summary: Adam Rank catches you up on the vital information and insight needed to make tough lineup decisions in Week 4.
stories.body:
The NFL returns to London this week when the Washington Commanders and Indianapolis Colts square off at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. The Commanders and Colts are middle of the pack in terms of offensive scoring, but being "mid" is a welcome relief in Tottenham, a club that didn't score their first goals of the English Premier League season until Week 4 against Liverpool. And it didn't score at home until the following week before the international break.

As we head into October, Tottenham is also still winless ... wait a minute, this is supposed to be a fantasy football column.

I will say this about Commanders QB Marcus Mariota, he finds a way to make Terry McLaurin more efficient. McLaurin has notched nine targets in back-to-back weeks, and he has a great matchup against the Colts, who have struggled against the pass this season. And isn't this what Sauce Gardner was supposed to prevent? McLaurin is a great WR2 start this week. On the other side, Josh Downs should have a good opportunity against the Commanders who have given up a league-leading six touchdown receptions to the position this season.

I know it's tough to get up early for these games (though U.S. fans of the EPL are veterans at this), but you're going to want to see this show. And if you're a Tottenham supporter, you're going to want to see people actually scoring in your stadium. Let's look at some other notes you need to know heading into Week 4.

Quarterback notes

What are we doing with our Los Angeles Chargers? Sorry, don't mean "our" like a team we support. But "our" as in players we (mistakenly) drafted. Justin Herbert might still be a start for you because most of the good quarterbacks have already been streamed off waiver. Herbert has yet to top 250 passing yards in a game this season. He has gone four consecutive games with one or no touchdowns dating back to last season. I've made the decision to move on from Herbert and will start Mariota this week, which will probably mean that Herbert will have the week of his life against the Seattle Seahawks in what will be Mike Macdonald's first time facing his former head coach at Michigan. I just can't stand the thought of playing Herbert again.
C.J. Stroud was another streaming option, considering the matchup against the Dallas Cowboys who just recently traded for Joey Porter Jr. The Cowboys have given up more than 27 points per game this season (25th). They have allowed a third-down conversion rate of 59%, which is the worst in the NFL. The matchup is there for Stroud, but there is just something about the Houston Texans' offense that doesn't sit right with me. The return of Nico Collins would help, but I'd rather stick with Mariota or Sam Darnold in desperate times.
Kyler Murray is a top-10 quarterback this week for me, with or without Justin Jefferson. And you can almost reason that the Minnesota Vikings would be better served to just keep Jefferson on the bench because it's the Miami Dolphins. Still, Murray has a 70.6 Total QBR against AFC teams in his career, the second-highest Total QBR against AFC teams since he entered the league in 2019. I'll give you one guess who is first ... and you're right, it's Patrick Mahomes.

Running back notes

The Dolphins' running back situation makes me sad. Ollie Gordon II was a top waiver-wire add this week, but I don't know how you can get him into your lineup. I'd start him over Isaiah Davis, Blake Corum and Woody Marks, for instance, but that's not exactly what you call a glowing recommendation. It's sort of like trying to pick out the best sushi roll at the gas station.
Did the Pittsburgh Steelers expose the Cincinnati Bengals defense last week, or was that a one-week thing? I don't know, I'm kind of worried that the Bengals' defense (that looked great the first two weeks of the season) is regressing. Aaron Rodgers threw for three touchdowns and the Bengals also gave up 138 rushing yards. This feels as if we could have the Bhayshul Tuten breakout game a lot of fantasy analysts have been beginning for.
There was concern Jeremiyah Love was going to be eased into the Arizona Cardinals' offense, because there wasn't much to play for. But the Cardinals have been frisky so far this season, as Love has had career highs in attempts (20), rushing yards (90) and receptions (five) against the San Francisco 49ers. And I know his NFL career has been three games. Still, show me the lie -- those are career highs.

Wide receiver notes

Green Bay Packers WR Christian Watson has four receiving touchdowns, the highest total along with Seattle's Jaxon Smith-Njigba. But I'm telling you, Matthew Golden needs to be started. Golden has 253 receiving yards this season (eighth most). He needs 109 more receiving yards to surpass his total of 361 from last season.
I get a lot of questions about the Chicago Bears' receiving room moving forward. Most seem to agree Luther Burden III is the No. 1 receiver in the offense. Which, fine. I'll concede that point as he does lead the team in targets. But has Kalif Raymond moved past Rome Odunze as the team's No. 2 receiver? Raymond leads the Bears in receptions (19) and receiving yards (214). Odunze leads the team in routes run. He's third in the NFL in targeted air yards (17.2). And the fact remains, had he come down with that ball in the end zone, nobody is wrong about his fantasy statistics. But as a Bears supporter who watches the games with a little more emotion, it's easy to see Raymond is coming up with clutch plays. That said, I'm not starting Raymond this week, but he's on my roster.

Tight end notes

The point about Odunze also extends to Colston Loveland, in that if he had extended the ball over the goal line, those six points put him on another level among tight ends. He didn't. But he's still used in the same way in this offense. He's heavily involved and the big game is coming soon. The Jets are a tough defense, but I'm not going to trust any waiver wire target tight end to take his starting spot in my lineup. Loveland it is.

stories.headline: Sir Alex Ferguson was 'terrified' about Old Trafford return after brain surgery
stories.summary: Sir Alex Ferguson has revealed he was "terrified" when returning to Old Trafford for the first time following brain surgery in 2018.
stories.body:
Sir Alex Ferguson has revealed he was "terrified" when returning to Old Trafford for the first time following brain surgery in 2018.

The former Manchester United manager, now 84, suffered a brain haemorrhage at the age of 76 and returned to the stadium four months later to watch them play Wolves in the Premier League.

"I was terrified actually," Ferguson told BBC Breakfast. "I wish I could say I was comfortable. I wasn't."

Ferguson and late wife Cathy were given a standing ovation when taking their seats in the directors' box.

"My wife was with me, and she was nearly crying," Ferguson said. "When we sat down, she said, 'that's fantastic.'"

Ferguson had retired as United boss five years before his brain haemorrhage, having won 36 major trophies during his 26-year spell in charge.

He also spoke about his fear after being left unable to talk in the days following his surgery.

"I had lost my voice. I couldn't speak," he said. "That was a frightening moment. I remember my grandsons coming to see me and I had lost my voice.

"Then they brought in a therapist and she started doing things like asking me to write down the names of birds, names of animals, names of rivers. That way my voice came back."

Lewis Hamilton
At the time, Hamilton was a three-time world champion, having won his first title with McLaren in 2008 before adding two more with Mercedes in 2014 and 2015. He would win a fourth in 2017 -- and returns to Malaysia nine years later with seven titles to his name.

During the race nine years ago he finished second to Verstappen, who was in his second season at Red Bull at the time.

Hamilton shares the record for most poles at Sepang with Michael Schumacher, with five each, and he was the last driver on the current grid to take pole here.

Charles Leclerc
The Monégasque was racing in Formula 2 with Prema Racing and was the runaway leader at the time.

Leclerc did, however, get a taste of an F1 weekend as -- not for the first time -- he competed in FP1 in place of Marcus Ericsson. He was three-tenths quicker than Pascal Wehrlein.

Leclerc went on to win the F2 drivers' championship that same year, earning himself a spot in the highest tier of motorsport a year later as a full-time F1 driver for Sauber.

Kimi Antonelli
The Mercedes driver, who is currently leading the drivers' championship and is on course to be the youngest to hold the title, has never raced in Malaysia. He was karting in Europe at the time and was only 11 years old.

Antonelli, now 20, is 66 points ahead of teammate George Russell and has eight career victories in what is only his second season in F1.

George Russell
In 2017, the Englishman was racing in GP3 with ART Grand Prix and went on to win the championship that year in his rookie season.

He later made his F1 debut for Williams in 2019, so missed out on racing in Malaysia by two years.

Fernando Alonso
Alonso, who is now the oldest driver on the grid at 45 years old, was racing for McLaren-Honda in 2017.

At the time he was driving an uncompetitive car and finished the season 15th in the title standings, scoring points in only five races.

In Malaysia, he finished outside the points in 11th.

Lance Stroll
The Canadian has been in F1 for longer than most on the grid and was racing for Williams at the time. He finished eighth and picked up four points in what was his rookie season.

Alex Albon
Albon was regularly racing against Leclerc in F2 for ART Grand Prix in 2017. He finished his rookie season in 10th and two years later he made his F1 debut for Toro Rosso.

After a stint at Red Bull and a year as its reserve driver, he then signed for Williams in 2022 and has been there for the last five seasons. He joins the majority of the grid in racing in Malaysia for the first time.

Carlos Sainz

The Spaniard is one of the drivers who has raced here before when he was driving for Toro Rosso.

But it didn't last for long as he only completed half the race after suffering a power unit issue, which forced him to retire from seventh place.

Lando Norris

Norris was another driver who was racing -- and winning a title -- in a junior series, clinching the European Formula 3 championship with Carlin.

During the same year he joined McLaren's Driver Development Programme, before making his F1 debut in 2019 with the team.

Oscar Piastri

The Australian was competing in the F4 British Championship and ended up finishing the season second. He was racing for TRS Arden Junior Racing Team.

Esteban Ocon
Ocon, soon to be an F1 free agent, was racing for Force India at the last race here in 2017 and finished with a point in 10th.

Oliver Bearman
The young Briton was still karting in the UK. In 2017, he won the Kartmasters British Grand Prix in the Honda Cadet category at the age of 12

Max Verstappen

F1's four-time world champion was competing in his first full season for Red Bull after getting promoted early into 2016 after just one year under his belt at Toro Rosso.

He was only 20 years old at the time of the last race in Malaysia, but he won from third place after a dominant drive.

Verstappen passed Hamilton on Lap 4 and he was in control of the race from there.

Isack Hadjar

Hadjar joins the list as one of the youngsters who has never raced here. He was 13 years old at the time and was karting in France before progressing to the international scene.

Liam Lawson
New Zealander Lawson was competing in Australia in the Formula 4 Championship and ended up finishing second with his team BRM at the age of 15.

Arvid Lindblad

In 2017, Arvid Lindblad was competing in British karting championships, specifically racing in the cadet categories IAME Cadet and Honda Cadet.

Lindblad is the youngest driver on the current grid and was only nine at the time of the last Malaysian GP.

Franco Colapinto

Colapinto was competing at a high level in karting and won the Argentine Pre-Junior Karting Championship the year before.

In 2017, he won the Buenos Aires Regional Championship in the junior class, before moving to the UK to continue his racing career.

Pierre Gasly

Gasly made his Formula 1 debut at the 2017 Malaysian Grand Prix, replacing Daniil Kvyat at Toro Rosso, and finished 14th.

Nico Hülkenberg

Hülkenberg was racing for Renault and finished down in 16th. The German driver had previously been at Force India.

Gabriel Bortoleto

Bortoleto was racing for CRG Factory Team in the OK Junior karting category in Europe after making the move from Brazil. He was 12 at the time.

He became a full-time F1 driver with Sauber in 2025, ahead of the team's transition to Audi.

Sergio Pérez

The Mexican driver has raced in Malaysia seven times during his F1 career. In 2017, he was racing for Force India and finished the race in sixth.

Valtteri Bottas

Bottas was Hamilton's Mercedes teammate and started fifth on the grid, finishing in the same position.

stories.headline: A'ja Wilson scores 36 points as the Aces send the Fever home again with a 94-83 win in Game 3
stories.summary: — A'ja Wilson made sure her basketball spoke for itself Thursday night.
stories.body:
LAS VEGAS -- — A'ja Wilson made sure her basketball spoke for itself Thursday night.


The four-time WNBA MVP, who had a verbal encounter with a Fever fan in Indiana two nights earlier, scored 36 points and grabbed 10 rebounds to lead the defending champion Las Vegas Aces to a 94-83 victory in the deciding Game 3 of the first round.


“I have my moments because I'm human,” Wilson said. “But after a while, I understood I didn't want that to be a distraction to myself and my team, and I knew what we had to do coming into tonight. So I put it behind me. I prayed a lot. I cried a lot.”


The third-seeded Aces, who have won three of the past four titles, moved on to play the winner of the Golden State-Dallas series, which will be decided Friday night in San Francisco.


This is the second year in a row Las Vegas has ended the season for the Fever, who were seeded sixth. The teams met in the semifinals a year ago, with the Aces pulling out an overtime victory in the finale of the five-game series that Caitlin Clark missed because of injury.


“We've got to give credit to the Aces,” Clark said. “I thought they played well. I thought they were ready to go. That's what championship teams do.”


Wilson book ended this series with sensational performances in Games 1 and 3, making her sure verbal confrontation with a Fever fan wouldn't be the enduring memory. The league did not punish Wilson, who opened the series with 38 points and 16 rebounds, followed up in this game by scoring 21 points in the first half and making 11 of 18 shots overall.


Teammate Chelsea Gray added 23 points and Jackie Young had 18 points, eight rebounds and seven assists.


Clark scored 11 points in the first quarter, but was held to seven the rest of the game. Kelsey Mitchell led Indiana with 23 points but shot 7 for 23. Aliyah Boston had 19 points and 10 rebounds.


Tensions ran high again Thursday, both teams bringing the physical play expected when each season is on the line in a game that had the intensity of a WNBA Finals.


Clark and Las Vegas' Brianna Turner each picked up a technical foul just more than three minutes into Game 3. The Fever were huddling on the court when Turner worked her way into the group only to be shoved out by Clark.


Early in the second quarter, Indiana coach Stephanie White was called for a technical, arguing that Turner brought down Lexie Hull, who instead picked up the foul.


Clark took a shot to her mouth in the fourth quarter and had to be attended to because of the blood.


The Aces threatened to run away from Indiana in the third quarter, taking a 67-55 before going cold over the final 4:32 and making just one shot. The Fever twice cut their deficit to two points in the fourth to make Las Vegas sweat out the ending.


Aces forward Stephanie Talbot, who started all but one game this season, did not play because of a leg injury and was replaced by Jewell Loyd, who scored 11 points. Talbot averaged 8.5 points and 3.5 rebounds in the first two games of this series.


Las Vegas coach Becky Hammon said she didn't know what Talbot's status would be going forward.


“She was a game-time decision,” Hammon said. “I just told her, ‘You’ve got to do what's best for your body.' Her assignment in this particular game is such a huge one if she's not at 100%, I need to see somebody at 100%. I know she was heartbroken she couldn't get out there and physically get it done.”

stories.headline: St. Louis up to 2nd place with unbeaten run now at 17 games
stories.summary: Simon Becher and Tomas Ostrak each scored late in the second half as St. Louis City SC beat the New York Red Bulls 3-0 on Wednesday night.
stories.body:
Simon Becher and Tomas Ostrak each scored late in the second half as St. Louis City SC beat the New York Red Bulls 3-0 on Wednesday night.

St. Louis (13-6-8) extended its unbeaten streak to 17 matches in MLS play and moved up to second place in MLS' Western Conference table.

New York (9-12-6) entered having conceded just two goals in its last four games, with Ethan Horvath recording three shutouts.

The Red Bulls had won their last two games, but were without rising stars Adri Mehmeti and Julian Hall for the game, with the pair away on national team duty for the United States.

Rafael Navarro opened the scoring just five minutes into the game when he redirected Conrad Wallem's header across the goal.

Becher capitalized on a New York turnover deep in its own half to make it 2-0 in the 87th minute. Ostrak sent in a rebound in stoppage time.

Roman Bürki made four saves to earn his third clean sheet of the season for St. Louis.

It was the first time New York and St. Louis have met during the regular season.

St. Louis hosts the LA Galaxy next on Oct. 11, while the Red Bulls play San Diego FC at home the day before.

stories.headline: Toby Greene joins Geelong on day one of AFL free agency
stories.summary: The AFL has revealed Greater Western Sydney's compensation draft pick after former skipper Toby Greene completed his late-career move to Geelong.
stories.body:
Toby Greene has become the first major AFL free agency domino to fall, with Greater Western Sydney to receive a second-round draft pick for losing their former captain to Geelong.

The Cats lodged paperwork on Friday to land the inaugural Giant as an unrestricted free agent.

Greene, a triple All Australian and dual club champion, booted 450 goals across his 15-year, 282-game tenure for GWS.

The 33-year-old cited family reasons for returning to his native Victoria and reunites with his close mate and former Giants forward Jeremy Cameron at the Cattery on a lucrative three-year deal.

The Giants will receive a second round draft selection as compensation, currently slated at No.26.

Earlier, key forward Joel Amartey's switch from Sydney to Carlton was confirmed as the free agency period opened.

The Swans will receive draft compensation for losing the unrestricted 27-year-old, who was an emergency during finals after failing to convince coach Dean Cox following a partial Achilles tear.

Paperwork will be lodged later on Friday to rubber stamp Lachie Neale's move to Collingwood as an unrestricted free agent after the Brisbane Lions star added a third premiership medal to his swag of silverware.

Melbourne's 2021 premiership vice-captain Jack Viney is poised for a move with two years remaining on his contract after meeting with West Coast.

After being sidelined through injury for all but one game this season, the 32-year-old was told by coach Steven King there would likely be limited opportunities for him in the Demons midfield.

"Footy's gone that way mate," Viney told 10 News at Perth Airport on Thursday.

"So took a bit to process early days, but we're here now, so we'll make the best of the opportunity ... it (a deal) will get done."

Young Hawthorn forward Calsher Dear, meanwhile, has opted to stay at the Hawks on a two-year deal after weighing up a potential move to the Dees.

The 21-year-old, son of late 1991 Norm Smith medallist Paul Dear, burst onto the scene in his debut season with 25 goals from 17 appearances in 2024.

But the emerging tall has struggled to hold his spot through injury and internal competition, adding just 14 games in 2025 and 2026.

"We are very excited about what the future holds for Calsher with a strong pre-season under his belt and greater continuity into 2027 and beyond," Hawks list manager Mark McKenzie said.

Hawthorn's key forward selection squeeze is set to worsen in 2027, with Gold Coast's restricted free agent Ben King expected to join Jack Gunston, Mitch Lewis, Mabior Chol and Dear.

The next night, when the fight concluded with Perez announced as the winner, Dumont appeared shocked by the unanimous decision and Perez turned her back on Dumont and twerked in her direction. The fighters had to be separated again before being escorted from the cage.

The fight that happened in between those fiery moments? It was not nearly as fierce. It began with a Round 1 in which Dumont landed eight significant strikes and Perez only four. And while the action picked up a little in the two rounds that followed, the women mostly circled each other.

But Perez got the win, and as a result, she moved up two spots to No. 2 in the ESPN women's bantamweight rankings, bumping Dumont down to No. 3.

stories.headline: Bruise Crew: Knights duo settle on nickname
stories.summary: Newcastle's rising back-rowers Francis Manuleleua and Jermaine McEwen want their own identity and have shunned the 'Bash Brothers' moniker.
stories.body:
The emergence of the raw-boned back-row duo of Jermaine McEwen and Francis Manuleleua has been critical to Newcastle's run to the NRL grand final.

But as commentators look for a nickname that best sums up the Knights' gruesome twosome, the pair are clear that they don't want to be known as a cheap imitation of what's gone before.

"We don't want to be called the Bash Brothers, because that's already taken, we've got to figure something out," said McEwen.

'The Bash Brothers' was a moniker given to Penrith duo Moses Leota and James Fisher-Harris during the Panthers' run to four-straight premierships.

Penrith edge forwards Joe Galuvao and Tony Puletua were christened 'the Hair Bears' in 2003, while Canberra's devastating centre-wing combination of Joey Leilua and Jordan Rapana was dubbed 'Leipana' a decade ago.

So when a list of potential nicknames is put to McEwen and Manuleleua ahead of Sunday's clash against the Sydney Roosters, the duo settle on one name for their hard-hitting partnership.

"The Bruise Crew, I like that one," Manuleleua said.

It's a fitting tag for the pair, who have come from relative obscurity to feature in this year's decider all while trampling or folding anybody who stands in their way.

The 21-year-old McEwen, was running around in the Koori Knockout on grand final weekend last year.

McEwen, who only has 39 first grade games to his name, showed he won't be intimidated when he barked at Leota in the Knights' energy-sapping win over Penrith.

"You probably don't want to hang around us too much because we just muck around too much," Manuleleua said.

"But when it comes to training and game day, we flick that switch and we're just ready to bang."

Manuleleua is just 14 games into his NRL career and not so long ago the 22-year-old was mowing the grass outside Penrith's centre of excellence.

In last week's preliminary final win over the Panthers he scored the opening try and pulled off a terrific try-saver to stop Brian To'o.

McEwen hopes he and Manuleleua, who room together, will line up alongside each other for Samoa at the World Cup.

"We both lean on each other a lot with each other's energy," McEwen said.

"I was always burning energy thinking about the game and he's just a chill guy, but on gameday he's a beast, bro.

"We just love playing with each other because you bring that energy and want to go out there and bang."
